finding.claim: Caller identity is taken verbatim from the client-supplied X-Session-User-Verified header with no verification, so any client that can reach the app can impersonate any user listed in a grants table and delete or rename their resources.
finding.source: HTTP request header X-Session-User-Verified (attacker-controlled), read in load_user() at views.py:11.
finding.sink: Authorization decisions on g.user: ensure_allowed(g.user, f, "delete") at views.py:17 (protects `del STORE[fid]` at views.py:18) and is_allowed(g.user, f, "write") at views.py:25 (protects the rename write at views.py:27).

trace.note: g.user = request.headers.get("X-Session-User-Verified"); no signature, token, or session lookup.
ensure_allowed(g.user, f, "delete") passes the spoofed identity through.
is_allowed: action in resource.get("grants",{}).get(user, []); true whenever the spoofed name is a key with "delete" in its list.
abort(403) only when the check fails.
del STORE[fid] executes for the impersonated user. Same flow for rename at views.py:24-27 via is_allowed(g.user, f, "write").

finding.guards_checked: (1) before_request (views.py:9-11): sets identity only, no authentication, no verification of the header or its origin. (2) No signing, JWT, or session cookie check anywhere in the repo. (3) acl.py is_allowed uses exact dict key and list membership, so no bypass of the grant check itself is needed; the attack works by choosing a valid user name. (4) No proxy or gateway configuration exists in this repo, so I could not verify that an upstream strips or overwrites this header. Exploitability depends on this: if the app is reachable without a trusted proxy that sets the header, the bug is directly exploitable; if it is only reachable through a proxy that overwrites the header on every request, the risk drops substantially. Usernames must be known (grant keys are probably emails or IDs, often guessable).

verdict.guard_found: none. load_user (views.py:9-11) only copies the header into g.user with no authentication or signature check. ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10) aborts on failure, but the identity it checks is the attacker-supplied header, so it passes for any granted name. is_allowed at views.py:25 is tested, but it also uses the same spoofed g.user. The repo contains no proxy or gateway config that would strip or overwrite the header.
verdict.reason: The app trusts the client-supplied X-Session-User-Verified header at views.py:11 with no check, so an anonymous caller who knows a name in the grants table passes ensure_allowed at views.py:17 and reaches the delete at views.py:18 (rename via views.py:25 and :27 likewise). This holds only if the app is reachable without a trusted proxy that overwrites the header, which the repo cannot show, so it is a deployment-dependent but direct flaw as written.

finding.claim: Unknown file IDs raise an unhandled KeyError (HTTP 500) while existing files the caller cannot access return 403, so the status code is an existence oracle for file IDs.
finding.source: URL path parameter fid (attacker-controlled), views.py:14-16 and views.py:22-24.
finding.sink: STORE[fid] lookup at views.py:16 and views.py:24, with the 403-vs-500 response difference produced by ensure_allowed (acl.py:9-10) and the uncaught KeyError.

trace.note: f = STORE[fid]; a missing key raises KeyError before any authorization check.
Not reached for a missing key, so no 403 is returned.
abort(403) is returned for an existing object the caller lacks rights to.
Rename path has the same lookup-before-check ordering.

finding.guards_checked: No 404 handling and no uniform error response. Only before_request sets the identity, and that does not gate lookups. Impact is low: it requires guessable IDs, and the status code alone reveals nothing about file contents. Also flagged as a logic flaw: the object is loaded before the authorization decision, so the same not-found and forbidden responses are not indistinguishable.

verdict.guard_found: None. The only before_request hook (views.py:9-11) sets g.user from a request header and gates nothing. The lookup at views.py:16 and views.py:24 has no try/except or 404 handling, so a missing key raises KeyError before any check. ensure_allowed (acl.py:8-10) aborts with 403 only for existing objects, and rename_file (views.py:25-26) returns 403 only after the lookup. The 403-vs-500 difference is therefore observable by any caller, including anonymous ones.
verdict.reason: The trace is accurate: a missing ID raises KeyError at views.py:16 and returns 500, while an existing ID the caller cannot access reaches abort(403) at acl.py:10 via views.py:17, and the same ordering holds at views.py:24-26, so any caller can distinguish existing from non-existing file IDs. The impact is low (existence disclosure only, and only for guessable IDs), but the claim as stated holds.
